description:
You are analyzing your school timetable for the week. Each day has multiple periods, and each period has a subject. You want to count how many times each subject occurs in a week.

Instructions:

    ["Math", "History", "English", "PE"],
    ["Math", "English", "Chemistry", "Art"],
    ["Physics", "Math", "English", "Music"],
    ["Biology", "Math", "English", "Drama"],
    ["Math", "English", "History", "PE"]
]

• Use a dictionary to count how many times each subject appears in the week.

• Identify most frequent subject(s) and least frequent subject(s).

• Print a summary report with:

• Each subject and its total count

• The most frequent subject

• The least frequent subject

Hints:

• Loop through days and then periods to update the dictionary.

• Use max() and min() with key=dictionary.get to find most/least frequent subjects.

NOTE:  Using max() and min() with key=books_read.get

When you have a dictionary where the keys are items (friends’ names) and the values are counts (books read), you can find the friend who read the most or least books.

Example Dictionary

books_read = {
    "Alice": 12,
    "Bob": 8,
    "Charlie": 15,
    "Diana": 10
}

Goal

• Find the friend who read the most books → Charlie

• Find the friend who read the least books → Bob

How max() works

Normally, max(dictionary) returns the largest key alphabetically:

print(max(books_read))  # Output: 'Diana' (alphabetical max)

This is not what we want. We want the key with the largest value.

Solution: key=books_read.get

most_books = max(books_read, key=books_read.get)
least_books = min(books_read, key=books_read.get)

Step-by-step explanation using books_read.get(key):

•
books_read.get(key) returns the value associated with a key (number of books read).

•
max(books_read, key=books_read.get) works like this internally:

# Pseudo-step-by-step
for key in books_read:
    value = books_read.get(key)   # Get the number of books
# Compare values and pick the key with the largest value

•
min(books_read, key=books_read.get) works similarly for the smallest value.

name: Challenge #59: Writing Files - Write a program to encrypt files
module: Class 4: Reading and Writing a File
description:
You are asked to create a program that can encrypt text files. Students can choose one of the following encryption methods:

Caesar Cipher (Simple Shift Cipher)

•
Concept: Shift each letter in the text by a fixed number of positions in the alphabet.

•
Example: With a shift of 3:

A → D, B → E, C → F

Vigenère Cipher (Shifting by a Keyword)

•
Concept: Use a keyword to determine the shift for each letter. Each letter of the keyword corresponds to a shift for the text letter at the same position.

•
Example:

Text:    H  E  L  L  O
Keyword: K  E  Y  K  E

Calculation:

H (7) + K (10) = 17 → R
E (4) + E (4)  = 8  → I
L (11) + Y (24) = 35 → 35 % 26 = 9 → J
L (11) + K (10) = 21 → V
O (14) + E (4) = 18 → S

•
Encrypted Text: RIJVS

Substitution Cipher (Using a Substitute Alphabet)

•
Concept: Replace each letter in the text with a different letter or symbol according to a mapping.

•
Example:

Original alphabet:    ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
Substitute alphabet:  QWERTYUIOPASDFGHJKLZXCVBNM
Text: HELLO → ITSSG

Google these ciphers if you need more details.

Challenge Instructions:

• Ask the user for:

•
Input file name (text file to encrypt)

•
Output file name (file to save encrypted text)

•
Encryption method (Caesar, Vigenère, or Substitution)

• If Caesar Cipher: Ask for shift number.

• If Vigenère Cipher: Ask for keyword.

• If Substitution Cipher: Either generate a random mapping or let the user provide one.

• Encrypt the content of the input file using the chosen method:

• For Caesar and Vigenère, only letters are encrypted; punctuation and spaces remain unchanged.

• Substitution replaces letters according to the mapping.

• Write the encrypted content to the output file.

name: Challenge #500: Trip Expense Calculator & Bill Splitter
description:
Project Overview

You will create a Trip Expense Calculator for a group of friends going on a trip together.
Each person may spend money on different items such as food, transport, accommodation, or activities.

Your program will calculate how much everyone spent, find each person’s fair share, and suggest who should pay whom so that everyone ends up paying equally.

This project combines real-world logic with Python programming, testing your ability to use input/output, loops, dictionaries, and functions effectively.

Project Objectives

By completing this project, you will learn how to:

• Collect and process user input dynamically.

• Perform calculations using loops and dictionaries.

• Implement a greedy algorithm to minimize the number of payments.

• Display results neatly in a menu-driven interface.

• Modify and update data during program execution.

• Export the final results to a text file.

Key Technical Words Explained

Term
Meaning

Variable
A name that stores data (e.g., total_cost = 300).

Loop
Repeats a block of code, such as asking for multiple expenses.

Dictionary
A data structure that stores data in key-value pairs (e.g., "Alice": 120).

Function
A reusable block of code that performs a task (e.g., calculating balances).

Balance
The difference between how much someone spent and what they should have paid.

Greedy Algorithm
A step-by-step approach that always picks the best immediate option (like matching the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor).

Menu-driven interface
A program that shows a list of choices and lets the user select what to do next.

Exporting to a file
Writing results from the program into a .txt file so they can be saved or printed later.

Project Requirements

Input

• Ask for the number of participants.

• Ask for the name of each participant.

• Allow each participant to enter multiple expenses (e.g., food, transport, etc.).

• Stop accepting expenses when the participant types 'done'.

Processing

• Sum all expenses for each participant.

• Calculate total trip cost.

• Determine each person’s fair share (total cost ÷ number of participants).

• Calculate balances — how much each person owes or is owed.

• Suggest who should pay whom to settle balances using as few transactions as possible.

Output (Menu Options)

When the program finishes processing, it should display a menu that allows the user to:

•
Display the transaction table

• Show all transactions with clear column headings:
Transaction | Person | Amount

•
Change an amount

• Allow the user to update a specific person’s expense and automatically recalculate totals and balances.

• Show the total trip cost

• Show each person’s fair share and balance

•
Show suggested payments to balance expenses

•
Export results to a text file

• Save the full summary (totals, fair shares, balances, and suggested payments) into a file called something like trip_summary.txt.

• Exit the program

Understanding the Greedy Algorithm

When people owe each other money, there are many ways to settle debts.
The goal is to minimize the number of payments while making sure everyone pays their fair share.

A Greedy Algorithm solves this by following a simple idea:

• Find the person who owes the most (debtor) and the person who is owed the most (creditor).

• Have the debtor pay the creditor as much as possible (the smaller of the two amounts).

• Update their balances.

• Repeat until all balances are zero.

This method is called greedy because it always takes the best step at the moment.
It’s efficient and works very well for real-world money-splitting problems.

Example

Input Summary:

Number of participants: 3
Alice spends: 120
Bob spends: 60
Charlie spends: 90

Output (Menu Option 5 – Show Suggested Payments):

Total trip cost: $270.00
Each person's fair share: $90.00

Balances:
Alice: +$30.00
Bob: -$30.00
Charlie: $0.00

Suggested payments:
Bob pays Alice $30.00

Output (Menu Option 6 – Export Results):
A text file named trip_summary.txt should be created with the above summary inside.

• Item name

• Item price

• Item ID (unique identifier)

Methods to implement:

•
__str__() — return a readable string showing the item’s name, price, and ID

• Any other methods needed to support adding/removing items to/from the cart

3. Program Requirements

• Start by greeting the user.

• Display a list of grocery items they can choose from.

• Let the user add items to the cart or remove them.

• Let the user view their cart and totals at any time.

• Use inheritance if you see opportunities for shared behavior.

• Use method overriding to customize how objects are printed (__str__) or how totals are displayed.

Example Interaction

Welcome to the Online Grocery Store!

Available Items:
1. Apple - $1.50
2. Bread - $2.00
3. Milk - $3.00

What would you like to do?
1. Add item to cart
2. Remove item from cart
3. View cart
4. View totals
5. Checkout

> 1
Enter item ID to add: 1
Apple added to your cart!

> 3
Items in your cart:
Apple - $1.50

> 4
Total price: $1.50

Hints for Implementation

• The ShoppingCart class can store a list of Grocery objects.

• Override __str__ in Grocery to display items nicely.

• Use methods in ShoppingCart to update the number of items and total price automatically.

• Optional: add tax calculations in view_totals() or in a separate overridden method.

name: CROC 2020
Challenge #1000: Build Your Own Banking Program
description:
Objective:

You will design and create a console-based banking program using Python and object-oriented programming. Your program will simulate a bank, allowing customers to create accounts, deposit and withdraw money, transfer funds, and keep track of all transactions. You will use classes, inheritance, and methods to organize your program.

Part 1: Create Your Account Classes

Students need to design a base class and at least three specialized account types:

•
BankAccount (Base Class)

• Attributes:

• Account number

• Account holder name

• Balance

• Transaction history (a collection of Transaction objects)

• Methods:

•
deposit(amount) – add money

•
withdraw(amount) – remove money

•
get_balance() – show current balance

•
display_account_info() – show account details

•
SavingsAccount (inherits BankAccount)

• Represents a savings account that earns interest.

• Additional method:

•
apply_interest() – calculate and add interest to the balance

•
CheckingAccount (inherits BankAccount)

• Represents an account for everyday spending.

• Additional feature:

• Allow overdraft: withdrawals can go beyond the current balance up to a limit

•
BusinessAccount (inherits BankAccount)

• Represents a small business account.

• Additional features:

• Store a business name

• Add bonuses for large deposits

Tip: Use inheritance to avoid repeating code for common features like deposits, withdrawals, and balance display.

Part 2: Create a Transaction Class

•
Transaction is a separate class that stores information about each financial action.

• Attributes of a Transaction:

• Type: "deposit", "withdrawal", "transfer in", or "transfer out"

• Amount

• Date and time

• Each account should maintain a transaction history, which is a data structure of Transaction objects.

• Students can choose a data structure they find appropriate, such as a list, dictionary, or queue, to store the transactions.

Banking Context:
Banks record every deposit, withdrawal, and transfer. Transaction histories help customers track their money and prevent mistakes.

Part 3: Implement a Menu System

Your program should have a console menu that allows users to choose actions:

• Create a new account

• Deposit money

• Withdraw money

• Apply interest (SavingsAccount only)

• Transfer money between accounts

• View account details

• View transaction history

• Exit the program

Banking Context:
Menus simulate how real banks provide options for managing accounts. Students should design the menu so it repeats until the user chooses to exit.

Part 4: Add Realistic Banking Features

•
Input Validation

• Users cannot enter invalid amounts (negative numbers, letters instead of numbers).

• Withdrawals cannot exceed overdraft limits for CheckingAccounts.

•
Persistent Storage

• Save all account and transaction data to a file so it is not lost.

• Load data when the program starts.

•
Money Transfers Between Accounts

• Users can transfer money from one account to another.

• Transfers should also appear in both accounts’ transaction histories.

•
Account Search

• Users can find accounts by account number or holder name.

Part 5: Deliverables

• Python program files implementing accounts, transaction class, menu system, and all features.

• Example screenshots of the program running.
